description: AstroResponse: A passionate team of young innovators combining Artificial Intelligence, software development, and UI/UX design to build smart health monitoring solutions for astronauts on deep-space missions. Driven by curiosity and teamwork, we turn real-time biometric data into intuitive, life-saving insights for the future of human space exploration.
summary:
AstroResponse

AI-Assisted Eye-Health Screening and Decision Support for Astronauts

AstroResponse is a prototype web application designed to support astronaut eye-health monitoring during long-duration space missions, with a focus on Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS).

In microgravity, fluid shifts toward the head can contribute to changes in the eyes and optic nerve. These changes may affect astronauts' vision and create challenges for medical monitoring, especially during missions far from Earth.

AstroResponse allows users to upload retinal fundus images for AI-assisted screening using a Roboflow model, which classifies images into Normal, Papilledema, or Pseudopapilledema categories and provides a confidence score for human review. The platform also includes symptom check-ins, side-by-side image comparison, a scan-log interface, and an editable daily planning draft with customizable reminders.

Additionally, AstroResponse integrates timestamped public NOAA GOES proton data to provide space-weather context alongside eye-health information.

By bringing these features together in one platform, AstroResponse helps astronauts and flight surgeons review potential eye-health concerns, organize monitoring information, and support medical decision-making during long-duration space missions, including situations where communication with Earth may be delayed.

AstroResponse is a screening and decision-support prototype, not a diagnostic medical system.
details: AstroResponse AI-Assisted Eye-Health Screening and Decision Support for Astronauts 1. Project Overview AstroResponse is a prototype web application designed to support astronaut eye-health monitoring during long-duration space missions. It focuses on Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), a condition associated with changes in the eyes and optic nerves during spaceflight. In microgravity, body fluids shift toward the head, which can contribute to optic disc swelling, retinal folds, and changes in the shape of the back of the eye. These changes may affect astronauts' vision and create challenges for medical monitoring, especially during missions far from Earth. AstroResponse brings several eye-health monitoring and decision-support features together in one platform, helping astronauts and flight surgeons review relevant information and organize follow-up. 2. How the Solution Works The prototype follows a simple workflow: 1. Retinal Image Upload Users upload a retinal fundus image (a photograph of the back of the eye) in JPG or PNG format, with a maximum size of 10 MB. The image is previewed locally before analysis. 2. AI-Assisted Image Screening After the user gives consent and selects "Analyze Image," the image is sent to a hosted Roboflow retinal classification model. The model returns one of three categories: - Normal - Papilledema - Pseudopapilledema The result also includes a confidence score. Papilledema refers to optic disc swelling, while pseudopapilledema can have a similar appearance without representing true swelling. The confidence score is provided for human review and should not be interpreted as diagnostic certainty. 3. Image Comparison and Symptom Check-ins Users can view a new retinal image beside an earlier reference image to support visual review. The platform also includes symptom inputs and a scan-log interface to help organize monitoring information during a session. 4. Space-Environment Context AstroResponse displays timestamped public NOAA GOES proton data alongside clearly labelled simulated readings. This provides environmental context about space-weather conditions, but does not represent an astronaut's personal radiation dose or actual spacecraft telemetry. 5. Daily Planning and Reminders The platform generates an editable daily planning draft with NASA-linked guidance and customizable reminders. These features are intended to help organize rest and mission-approved visual checks. 6. Human Review The information is presented for review by the crew member and flight surgeon. AstroResponse is a screening and decision-support tool, not a diagnostic system, and does not replace medical professionals or mission procedures. 3. NASA Data and Its Role NASA research resources provided the scientific foundation for AstroResponse. We used NASA's research on Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome to understand the effects of fluid shifts during spaceflight and identify relevant ocular findings, particularly optic disc swelling. NASA resources on eye-health research aboard the International Space Station also informed our decision to include retinal fundus-image screening. In addition, NASA-reported findings and prevalence figures were used in our project documentation to explain the importance of the problem and illustrate the frequency of SANS-related ocular changes. Alongside NASA research, the platform displays public NOAA GOES proton data as space-weather context. NOAA data is not a NASA dataset and is not used to calculate individual radiation exposure. 4. Tools, Technologies, and Software - Manus: An AI agent used to help build the prototype application and its interface. It also hosts the published web application. - Roboflow: Hosts the AI model used to classify uploaded retinal fundus images. - NOAA GOES public data: Provides timestamped space-weather context. - HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: Standard web technologies used to build the application, with parts of the code generated through Manus. - Web-based platform: The application is accessible through a browser on computers and mobile devices. - English and Arabic interface: Supports users in both languages. The current prototype does not require dedicated eye-imaging hardware; users upload existing fundus images. 5. What Currently Works The delivered prototype includes: - Fundus-image upload with local preview and a consent step before cloud analysis. - Roboflow-based image classification with three output categories and a confidence score. - Side-by-side comparison between a new image and an earlier reference image during the session. - Symptom inputs and a scan-log interface. - A context panel displaying labelled simulated readings and timestamped NOAA GOES proton data. - An editable daily planning draft and customizable reminders. - English and Arabic user interfaces. These features are demonstrated through screenshots of the working prototype in our project documentation. 6. Current Limitations AstroResponse is an early-stage prototype, and several limitations remain: - Scan history is not permanently stored, and authenticated medical-history management is not yet implemented. - The platform is not connected to medical eye-testing devices. - Image comparison is currently a visual, side-by-side review; it does not automatically calculate disease progression. - Simulated readings are not actual spacecraft telemetry. - NOAA proton data does not represent an astronaut's personal radiation dose. - The AI model's confidence score is not a medical diagnosis, and its accuracy has not been established in our project documentation. - The prototype has not been tested or clinically validated in spaceflight conditions. 7. Future Development Our future plans focus on expanding AstroResponse into a more comprehensive astronaut eye-health monitoring and decision-support platform. Planned improvements include: - Saved Medical History: Adding secure scan-history storage and authenticated medical records to support comparisons across multiple sessions. - Advanced Eye-Monitoring Integration: Connecting compatible visual-testing devices and additional ocular-health measurements. - Improved Environmental Monitoring: Integrating spacecraft environmental information, including cabin conditions such as CO2, and relevant dosimeter data when available. - Enhanced Medical Review: Developing a structured workflow for flight-surgeon review and mission-approved medical protocols. - Clinical Validation: Evaluating the retinal classification model using appropriate clinical fundus-image datasets and establishing its performance before any medical use. - Expanded Decision Support: Exploring how environmental and health information could be organized to support more informed, mission-specific medical review. Any future radiation-exposure analysis or personalized risk assessment would require validated dosimeter measurements, mission-specific data, and appropriate scientific models. 8. Expected Impact AstroResponse aims to contribute to safer long-duration human spaceflight by: - Making eye-health information easier for astronauts and flight surgeons to review. - Supporting the organization of retinal images, symptoms, and monitoring information. - Helping users identify image-classification results that may need further human review. - Providing relevant space-weather context alongside eye-health information. - Supporting more organized medical follow-up, particularly when communication with Earth is delayed. In the long term, we hope to develop AstroResponse into a more comprehensive health-monitoring and decision-support platform that can support astronauts during missions beyond low Earth orbit. AstroResponse is currently a screening and decision-support prototype. Its purpose is to support human review, not to diagnose medical conditions or independently make medical decisions.
